68:17.heading: Ayah 17

blocks.text: Indeed, We have tested them [i.e., the Makkans] as We tested the people of the garden when they swore to harvest its fruits in the early morning,

The story opens by declaring that a trial is taking place. Blessings themselves are a field of testing, just as Quraysh were tested through the blessings they had received. Some works of tafsir relate that the owners inherited their orchard from a righteous father who used to set aside some of its fruit for the poor. The sons continued his practice for a time before deciding to withhold that share. Yet the Quran does not begin with the history of the farm.

It begins at the more dangerous turning point: their intention to disobey became a firm resolve, an oath and a collective plan. They intended to harvest all the fruit early in the morning, before the poor arrived, leaving nothing for those accustomed to receiving their due. [The Arabic verb «يصرم» means to cut or harvest.] The opening thus reveals that a grave moral failure can begin before the act itself, when a deliberate decision to deprive someone of their right takes root in the heart.

68:18.heading: Ayah 18

blocks.text: and made no exception [by saying: if Allah wills][4].

[Two interpretations have been transmitted for the Arabic expression «ولا يستثنون»: they did not add ‘if Allah wills’, or they did not set aside any of the fruit for the poor—not even a single piece. A translation of the verse may convey only one of these meanings.] Both interpretations point to the same sense of self-sufficiency: disregarding Allah’s will and disregarding the right He has established over wealth. For years they had enjoyed a blessing they had not brought into existence themselves. They then treated it as their exclusive possession, acknowledging neither a Giver behind it nor a person in need with a claim upon it. Their ingratitude was already apparent in their plan, before their hands reached for the fruit.

68:19.heading: Ayah 19

blocks.text: Then it was struck by an affliction from your Lord while they were asleep,

The punishment came before they carried out their intention. [The opening Arabic particle «فـ» has been understood to suggest how swiftly the consequence followed their resolve and their oath to disobey.] Their plan could be overturned without any force they could see or resist. When Allah wills to destroy something, He has no need of a vast army. As He says: “After his death, We did not send down any soldiers from heaven against his people, nor would We have done so.” The following verse describes a single blast: “It was no more than a single blast, and immediately they were extinguished.” [The word «عليها», ‘over it’, is also understood here to suggest the extent of what befell the orchard.] They had intended to leave nothing for the poor; the calamity swept through the entire orchard and left them none of what they had planned to keep for themselves.

blocks.text: Their being asleep reveals how a person may devise plans and schemes, believing everything is settled, only for it all to be undone without their knowledge. Conversely, Allah may arrange good for an obedient servant without that person realizing it. The hadith about the owner of a garden provides an example. In that account, a man hears a voice in a cloud: “Irrigate the garden of so-and-so.” He follows the water until he reaches the garden and finds its owner.

The owner explains that he divides its yield into thirds: one for charity, one to feed himself and his family, and one to reinvest in the garden (Muslim, 2984). Just as that obedient man’s provision reached him through arrangements he could not see, this orchard was destroyed while its owners slept.

68:20.heading: Ayah 20

blocks.text: and it turned to ashes [as black as night].

The orchard’s condition precisely mirrors the owners’ intention. They meant to cut off the entire harvest from the poor, and the orchard itself became bereft of its produce. [The Arabic «يصرموا», ‘to cut or harvest’, and «الصريم» share a root. One explanation of «الصريم» is land that has turned black or lost its vegetation, leaving none of its expected yield.] The punishment corresponded to their intention: they wanted to cut others off from its benefit, so Allah cut them off from it. [The Arabic form «فعيل» in «صريم» is understood here to suggest a condition that had become established throughout the orchard, rather than temporary damage to part of the crop.] This fits what follows: when they saw it, they did not recognize it, and they later hoped their Lord would give them something better in its place.

68:21.heading: Ayah 21

blocks.text: Then in the early morning they called out to one another:

By this point the reader knows what has happened to the orchard, while its owners remain unaware. They awoke, each expecting the morning they had agreed upon, and began calling to one another. [The Arabic form «تنادوا» conveys reciprocal action: they called to each other.] This was neither one hesitant individual acting alone nor someone forced to go along. It was a group whose members stirred one another’s enthusiasm to carry out their decision. Here lies the danger when wrongdoing becomes a collective undertaking: instead of helping awaken another person’s conscience, a close companion helps entrench the plan and urges them to carry it through.

68:22.heading: Ayah 22

blocks.text: “Go early to your garden if you really wish to harvest.”

They urged one another to head early to their cultivated land if they truly intended to harvest it. The way they spoke of it reveals part of the mentality behind withholding: this is our effort, what we have worked hard for, the property we have made with our own hands. A person can become so impressed by their own efforts that they forget Who caused the crop to grow, preserved it and blessed it. [The Arabic «حرث», used here of cultivated land, is associated with working, earning and toil. The name Harith («حارث») comes from the same root.] This connection also appears in the hadith concerning truthful names: “the truest are Harith and Hammam” (Abu Dawud, 4950).

A human being works, earns and strives. But effort does not turn Allah’s gift into a possession independent of His command. Their challenge to one another about whether they truly meant to harvest also carried pressure: if you are serious, do not back down. A group may protect a wrong decision by mocking anyone who relents or making them feel less determined than the others, until returning to what is right comes to be regarded as weakness.

68:23.heading: Ayah 23

blocks.text: So they set out, whispering to one another,

Their setting out combined outward eagerness with inward secrecy. [One reflection on the Arabic «انطلقوا» draws on its association with release from a restraint: it is as though they regarded their former obedience and their father’s practice as a constraint from which they had finally found a chance to break free.] This attitude recurs when a person treats obedience as a burden whose end they await so they can return to what they desire.

68:24.heading: Ayah 24

blocks.text: “Not a single poor person should enter your garden today.”

Their whispered instruction marked the beginning of a new policy: no poor person was to enter that day, and nothing was to leave their wealth to satisfy the poor person’s right. [The Arabic «عليكم», literally ‘upon you’, is read here as reflecting their perception of a poor person as an intruder descending upon them, or an aggressor taking what is not theirs, rather than someone in need with a recognized claim.] This is the opposite of the Quranic measure, which describes the believers’ wealth as including a due for those who ask and those who are deprived: “and who give a due share[8] of their wealth” “to the beggar and the dispossessed;” (70:24–25). The fault was not simply that they gave too little in charity. Their whole understanding had been reversed: instead of seeing wealth as a blessing carrying an obligation, they saw a poor person as an intruder with no right to any of it.

68:25.heading: Ayah 25

blocks.text: And they left early, fully determined to stick to their plan[5].

They set out early, united in purpose, determination and confidence in their ability. The timing was calculated, the orchard was there, the fruit was ready and everyone agreed with the plan. To them, having all the means in place seemed to settle the outcome. Here is a hidden form of transgression: it lies not in using the means available, but in moving from using them to feeling that they make one independent of Allah. A person may think: the money is in my pocket, and what I want is before me, so why should I make the matter dependent on Allah’s will? Or they may assume that having money, a doctor and treatment guarantees the result. We are instructed to use the means available, but those means cannot prevent Allah from rendering them ineffective or put the outcome in their possessor’s hands.

68:26.heading: Ayah 26

blocks.text: But when they saw the garden, they said, “We must have lost our way!

The transformation was so complete that they looked at the land they had known for years and could not believe it was theirs. At first they thought they had taken the wrong road. What had happened was not merely a reduction in the quantity of fruit, but an immense change in something they had regarded as secure. This reinforces the understanding that the devastated state described in verse 20 applied to the whole orchard, not just a partial loss. A blessing so familiar that a person considers it a permanent part of life may change in a moment. They then see for themselves that long familiarity with something does not place it beyond Allah’s power.

68:27.heading: Ayah 27

blocks.text: Rather, we have been deprived.”

After the first shock, they came to understand the truth: they had been deprived. This is an important turning point in the story. Their understanding of what had happened led them to examine themselves; they did not settle for a purely material explanation that shut out self-examination. The existence of a natural cause does not negate Allah’s having decreed it at that time and in that form. This does not mean that every calamity can confidently be declared a specific punishment.

Rather, a person should not evade self-examination whenever something happens that might awaken them. Someone may explain every event by an external cause, or always attribute it to the evil eye or envy, and so lose an opportunity to reconsider their own conduct. These owners, however, understood that their deprivation was connected to what they had resolved to do. Recognizing the message was itself the beginning of their return to Allah.

68:28.heading: Ayah 28

blocks.text: The best among them said, “Did I not say to you to glorify Allah[6]?”

One of them reminded the others of his earlier warning to glorify Allah. [The Arabic «أوسطهم» has been interpreted as the one in the middle in age, or as the best and most just of them. The related word «وسط» also carries the sense of excellence in the description of the Muslim community in Quran 2:143.] He had voiced an objection and warned them before the punishment came, but that seed of goodness did not protect him because he ultimately went along with them. Merely suggesting to companions in wrongdoing that it would be better not to proceed, and then joining them, does not place a person outside the act. If a group rejects advice and persists, a sincere objection may require a practical break: refusing to take part. This reveals the danger of companionship that weakens a conscientious person’s resistance until they follow a course they already know to be wrong.

68:29.heading: Ayah 29

blocks.text: They said, “Glory be to our Lord! We were truly wrongdoers.”

They responded by glorifying their Lord and admitting that they had done wrong. Their glorification of Allah is closely connected to the root of their error. They had based their decision on the false belief that giving to the poor diminished wealth, while withholding what was due preserved and increased it. This was to think ill of Allah, Who has promised blessing and growth through obedience and says: “Allah destroys usury and nourishes charities, and Allah does not like any ungrateful sinner.” By glorifying their Lord, they rejected the false notion they had held about Him. By acknowledging their own wrongdoing, they placed the blame where it belonged: the fault was not in Allah’s judgment or in charity, but in their own understanding and conduct. Their return brought together a corrected understanding of Allah and an explicit admission that they had wronged themselves.

68:30.heading: Ayah 30

blocks.text: Then they turned to one another, throwing blame.

Once the plan collapsed, the fragility of the alliance behind it became apparent. Each began shifting responsibility onto someone else: one had suggested the idea, another had encouraged it, another had ignored the warning. But blame after the event neither restores the fruit nor erases anyone’s participation. Companions united in wrongdoing may spur one another on beforehand; when the consequences arrive, that encouragement turns into mutual accusation. It is therefore not enough to choose people who agree with us. We need someone who will turn us back when we are wrong, before everyone shares in the consequences.

68:31.heading: Ayah 31

blocks.text: They said, “Woe to us! We were surely transgressors.

Their mutual reproaches gave way to a deeper admission: they had transgressed. They did not describe their conduct merely as miserliness, but as transgression, because behind their refusal lay a sense of self-sufficiency. They thought they controlled the land, the plan and the timing, and could keep the wealth for themselves. This echoes the connection between transgression and feeling self-sufficient in the Quran: “Indeed, man transgresses” “when he deems himself to be self-sufficient.” When someone sees themselves as independent, their heart begins to lose its sense of the limits that servitude to Allah requires. They imagine that possessing the means makes them independent of the One Who causes those means to work. Yet Allah can nullify a means, prevent its effect, or make what they thought would bring benefit produce the opposite of what they intended.

68:32.heading: Ayah 32

blocks.text: Our Lord may give us something better than this. We certainly turn to our Lord in hope[7].”

Their hope for a better replacement reveals a change in the direction of their hearts. At the beginning, their desire was fixed on the fruit they wanted to keep for themselves. Once their weakness had been exposed, they turned in longing to their Lord. They did not claim a guaranteed right to have their orchard restored as it was. They hoped that Allah would give them something better in its place. Their repentance was thus more than grief over lost money: it restored their relationship with their Lord to its proper basis. The original gift comes from Allah, its replacement comes from Allah, and hope is attached not merely to the land but to the Lord of the land.

68:33.heading: Ayah 33

blocks.text: Such is the punishment [in this world]; but the punishment of the Hereafter is far worse, if only they knew.

The punishment in this world was severe, but it stopped them before they went further down their chosen path. They awoke to the truth, confessed their wrongdoing and returned to their Lord. Painful as it is, a worldly punishment may therefore open a door to mercy if it turns someone away from a course that would destroy them. Conversely, continued blessings while a person persists in disobedience do not necessarily mean that they are safe.

The Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, warned that when Allah continues to give a servant the worldly things they desire despite their persistence in sin, this is a gradual approach to punishment: “then [know] that it is only Istidraj from Allah Ta’ala.” [The Arabic term «استدراج» refers to being led gradually towards punishment while continuing to receive blessings.] He then recited Quran 6:44: “When they forgot the reminder that they were given[13], We opened for them the doors of everything – until when they rejoiced in pride for what they were given, We seized them by surprise, so they fell into utter despair.” The report is recorded by Ahmad, 17311, and has been graded hasan.
If this was the punishment of this world, the punishment of the Hereafter is greater. Awakening promptly to one’s error is therefore a blessing that should not be underestimated.

68:34.heading: Ayah 34

blocks.text: Indeed, the righteous will have gardens of bliss with their Lord.

After describing an orchard lost overnight when its owners resolved to withhold its produce from the poor, the Quran presents another measure: gardens of bliss await those who are mindful of Allah, with their Lord. The orchard’s owners feared losing some of what they held if they gave the poor their due, and they lost the whole orchard. Those mindful of Allah, however, are promised gardens with their Lord. This contrast turns the heart from immediate gain towards what lasts. A person who gives something up for Allah and fulfils their obligations does not measure success by how much fruit they have kept today, but by what Allah has stored up for them. An earthly garden may lose its yield in hours; the gardens of bliss are not subject to such loss.

68:35.heading: Ayah 35

blocks.text: Should We then treat Muslims like the wicked?

The question of whether those who submit to Allah should be treated like the guilty overturns a measure of success based on accumulating wealth and withholding it from others. Someone who submits to Allah, observes His limits and fulfils what is due to Him cannot be equated with someone who chooses transgression and wrongdoing, then demands the same outcome. The story is about more than the loss of an orchard: it redefines profit and loss. A person may retain something of this world yet be a loser before Allah, while another gives from their wealth for Allah and is the one who truly gains.

68:36.heading: Ayah 36

blocks.text: What is the matter with you that you make such a judgment?

The closing question challenges the judgments that produced their decision. How did they conclude that charity diminishes wealth, or that depriving the poor is a path to increase? How did they decide that possessing the means meant possessing the outcome? How did they rule out the fact that a blessing has a Giver Who can take it away? The fault began in their inner measure of things before it appeared in their conduct. Once their judgment about wealth, obedience and power became corrupt, their plan followed accordingly. The story thus addresses more than the act of miserliness: it addresses the way of thinking that produces it—how a person understands their possessions, the rights of those in need, Allah’s will and the meaning of true gain.
